results.title: Authenticating requests
results.snippet:
In order to make requests to the Attio REST API, you need to generate an access token. There are two ways to generate an access token:
1. By implementing an OAuth 2.0 flow
2. By generating an API key for your workspace
You should prefer the OAuth 2.0 flow if building an app for multiple workspaces. If you are building an app for a single workspace, you can manually generate an API key to make requests on behalf of that workspace only.
## Generating access tokens
### OAuth 2.0
Attio implements the standard [OAuth 2.0 specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749), using the Authorization Code Grant Flow ([RFC 6749 section 4.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-4.1)). You can find the reference for our OAuth authorize, token exchange and introspect endpoints [here](/docs/oauth/authorize). If you would prefer a tutorial on how to implement an OAuth 2.0 flow into an existing app, you can find one [here](/rest-api/tutorials/connect-an-app-through-oauth). We recommend using a well-established library for making OAuth requests, because they apply many of the security recommendations added after the original OAuth protocol was released. results.title: Authenticating to external services
results.snippet:
How to use connections in your app
1. Head to the **Connections** tab in your app’s settings, found in the [developer console](https://build.attio.com).
2. Configure a workspace and/or user connection for your app. Choose the type of connection that best suits the authentication requirements of your external service.
3. Retrieve the connection value in your server-side app code by calling either [`getUserConnection`](/sdk/server/connections/get-user-connection) or [`getWorkspaceConnection`](/sdk/server/connections/get-workspace-connection).
4. Use the connection value to authenticate to the external service when making HTTP requests.

Connection types
Attio currently supports the following authentication types:
- **Secret** - Stores a string secret, such as an API key.
- **OAuth 2.0** - Stores an OAuth 2.0 access token. Authentication to external services which support the [OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-4.1) is managed automatically by Attio.

results.snippet: Sign in Authentication Authentication The Attio API uses access tokens keys to identify and authorise calls to the developer API. Tokens can be generated in your Workspace settings. See this guide for more information on how to generate access tokens. Your API keys are able to authenticate to Attio and perform actions on your account so it's important that you keep them safe in the same way that you would a password. If you are building an integration for other Workspaces to use, we also provide OAuth flows for the Attio API. Please contact us for more information. Using Access Tokens We accept both Bearer and Basic HTTP Authentication. We recommend using Bearer Authentication. If you are using HTTP Basic Authentication, you should provide your API key as the Basic Authentication username. You can safely leave the password blank. If you are using HTTP Bearer Authentication you should provide your API key in the Authorization header as the Bearer value. To keep your API key secure you should always connect to the Attio API using HTTPS. Scopes Attio uses scopes to limit the access your integrations have to our API. 1. By implementing an OAuth 2.0 flow
2. By generating an API key for your workspace
You should prefer the OAuth 2.0 flow if building an app for multiple workspaces.

OAuth for unpublished apps
While you develop your app, it can grant tokens for the workspace it is installed in. To get access tokens for other workspaces, you’ll need to share your app with those workspaces or publish it. An unpublished app can be installed in up to 25 workspaces. See [installation limit](/share/private-invites#installation-limit) for more information. Before your app has an approved release, the version that an OAuth install gets depends on whether the workspace had a development install of your app before. See [OAuth flows for unpublished apps](/share/the-publication-lifecycle#oauth-flows-for-unpublished-apps).

results.title: Working with activities
results.snippet:
## Required scopes
The activity APIs use two [scopes](/rest-api/guides/authentication):
- `activity_configuration` for reading and writing activities themselves and their attributes.
- `activity_record` for reading and writing activity records.
Activity records link to object records, so the activity record endpoints additionally require `activity_configuration:read`, `object_configuration:read` and `record_permission:read`. Creating referenced records as part of a write also needs `record_permission:read-write`.
## Creating an activity
Create an activity with `POST /v2/activities`. Besides a slug and its display names, you must pick the [schema](/docs/activities#schemas) the activity extends: `activities`, `interactions`, `calls` or `emails`. When creating custom activities, it’s good practice to prefix the slug with an app-specific prefix like `{app_name}_site_visits` to prevent conflicts.
The response contains the new activity, including the schemas it directly extends:
The choice of schema is permanent: `PATCH /v2/activities/{activity}` can update the slug and nouns, but rejects `extends` with a `400`. You can list all activities with `GET /v2/activities` and fetch a single one

results.title: Filtering and sorting
results.snippet:
Attio supports two distinct formats for filtering. There is the verbose format, which supports a wider variety of operators and conditions, and a shorthand format, which is useful for quick equality checks.
### Shorthand filters
Shorthand filters generally look like this:
People called with the email
```
POST /v2/objects/companies/records/query
Content-Type: application/json
{
"filter": {
"name": "John Smith",
"email_addresses": "john@smith.com"
}
}
```

We have examples of filtering by each attribute type in our [attribute types documentation](/rest-api/attribute-types/attribute-types).

Attio MCP is Attio’s hosted MCP server that gives AI tools secure access to your Attio workspace. It’s designed to work seamlessly with popular AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more.
### Why use Attio MCP?
- **Easy setup** — Connect through simple OAuth with one-click installation for supported AI tools

- **Optimized for AI** — Built specifically for AI agents with efficient data formatting and human-readable responses
- **Secure by design** — Authenticates as your Attio user with OAuth, and read operations are auto-approved while write operations request confirmation

Your AI tools can read from Attio and write back to it, over Universal Context — the deepest context layer in agentic CRM — with access scoped to each person and actions verified before they run.
## What is Attio's MCP server?
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI tools to the systems they need. Attio's MCP server makes your workspace available to any MCP client, so the tool you already have open can read from Attio and write back to it.
It combines three things:
- **Speaks your language.** No views to build, no filters to set. Get insights and take action in conversation.
- **Full workspace access.** Search, create, and update across your CRM records and activities.
- **Secure by design.** Authenticate via OAuth with user-scoped permissions.
The result: your CRM stops being a place you always have to go and becomes something your AI tools can always reach, in every tool your team already works in.

Attio MCP connects external AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT to your Attio workspace, so you can search your CRM, update records, log notes, and manage tasks in natural language from wherever you already work with AI.

**MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI assistants securely interact with other systems. Your AI assistant connects to Attio's MCP server, you sign in with your Attio account, and the assistant can then use a set of Attio tools: searching records, creating and updating records, working with notes and tasks, managing views, and reading emails and meeting data.
See the [full list of the Attio MCP’s tools](https://docs.attio.com/mcp/overview#supported-tools).
Three things are worth understanding before you connect:
- **It acts as you.** The AI assistant authenticates as your Attio user through OAuth. It can only see and change what your own permissions allow.

# Attio
Cursor plugin that connects agents to [Attio](https://attio.com) through Attio's official remote [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server.
Search, create, and update CRM records (people, companies, deals, and custom objects), work with lists, notes, and tasks, and search emails, meetings, and comments in the signed-in Attio workspace.
## Install
1. Open **Cursor Settings → Plugins**.
2. Search for **Attio**.
3. Click **Install**, then complete the Attio sign-in prompt.
Or run `/add-plugin attio` in chat.
## MCP
```json
{
"mcpServers": {
"attio": {
"type": "http",
"url": "https://mcp.attio.com/mcp"
}
}
}
```
Auth is OAuth against Attio. Cursor prompts for Attio user login when the plugin connects — there is no API key or client ID to configure.
## Before you connect
You need an Attio account with access to a workspace. Attio MCP is available to all workspace members.
